lens: Art direction / anti-generic — does this brief produce a site with a point of view, or a very well-argued default?
verdict: This is the most rigorous generic site I have read. It knows every 2026 tell and dodges all of them, and the dodging is the disease: three of the four arguments for the chosen direction are negative ("not cream", "not a warm serif", "not corporate"), and a direction defined by avoidance converges on the average of whatever is left standing. In 2026 that average is exactly this — cool near-monochrome ground, one desaturated teal, hairlines at full ink, mono metadata, zero shadow, zero radius, a left-hand year rail, sidenotes, and a colophon. That is not neutral ground, it is the current attractor basin, and five of the eight reference sites (Asterisk, Works in Progress, gwern, Heer, Tufte CSS) are already sitting in it. The brief takes one CSS detail from each and calls the collage a direction. Meanwhile the one genuinely original idea in the document — accents lifted from the IPCC AR6 precipitation ramp so the interface and the figures share one scientific palette — is capped at "~2% of painted pixels", and its second half, the divergent dry pole, is spent on a single outbound-link arrow glyph. The typography is the safe triad of the genre: Source Serif 4 is gwern's own font, cited as such in the brief; IBM Plex Mono is the Inter of monospace; Public Sans is a face engineered to have no opinion. The site's only asymmetry evaporates below 1100px, where the largest and worst-served audience actually lives. The signature ornament — the one object on this site that no other site on earth could have — is specified at 8% opacity behind a hero, which is wallpaper. And the sample copy, which explicitly promises to preserve his slightly-off article usage, contains none of it and closes two consecutive paragraphs on the short-declarative reversal ("The answer, repeatedly, is that the gap is not in the models. It is in the observations." / "It is not finished.") that is the single most recognisable machine cadence of the last two years. Credit where it is due: the alumni placement column, the trainee marks, the Scholar/Highwire constraints, the failure-mode table, and self-hosting upstream for smcp/onum are real work and I would keep every one. But nothing in §3 or §4 is unjustifiable, and taste is by definition the part you cannot justify. A document in which every single choice has a citation, a ratio, or a licence clause behind it is a document optimised for surviving review, not for being looked at. Blurred to 20px — the brief's own test 16, which it specifies and never runs — the home page is a masthead bar, a left-heavy text block beside a portrait, a tinted callout, four stacked grey bands, and a 2×2 of rectangles. That is a well-made personal site. It is not his.

issues.problem: Eight references, five of which are the same genre (Asterisk, Works in Progress, gwern, Jeff Heer, Tufte CSS), each contributing one CSS detail. That is an average of a monoculture, and averaging is precisely the operation you are trying not to look like. The brief invokes 'an operational forecast bulletin' and 'a tide-gauge chart' in its mood line and then takes not one structural move from either. Zero references from hydrographic charts, USGS topo sheets, IMD/CWC bulletins, NWS AHPS river pages, Indian print, or scientific atlas design.
issues.fix: Cut three of the five text-web references and replace them with primary sources from his own discipline, and steal structure rather than CSS. From an NWS AHPS river forecast page: the stage-category band system (action/minor/moderate/major) and the 'ISSUED 0630 IST' teletype line — put that issue-stamp in mono caps at the top of every page as the last-updated. From a USGS topographic sheet: hydrography is labelled in blue italic serif — so every named water body on this site (Musi, Godavari, Narmada, Hussain Sagar, Osman Sagar) renders in italic in the accent, sitewide, automatically, via a build-time term list. From a hydrographic chart: the datum line — the site's section hairline is not decoration, it is a level, and it is drawn at the same y-position the hydrograph's flood-stage threshold sits at.

issues.problem: Source Serif 4 + Public Sans + IBM Plex Mono is the safe triad of exactly this genre. The brief chooses gwern's body font, citing gwern, then claims the result is a fingerprint. IBM Plex Mono is the most-used 'designer-y' mono of the past eight years. Public Sans is Libre Franklin with the character sanded off by a government style guide — it was literally designed to have no voice. Three OFL, GitHub-hosted, US-institution faces: zero risk and zero signature. The stated rationale (smcp/onum/tnum survive upstream subsetting) argues for self-hosting, not for these three faces — plenty of characterful OFL families have the same feature set.
issues.fix: Two families, not three — drop the sans entirely. Metadata, nav and captions go to the mono (the Works in Progress move the brief already cites); photo credits go to serif italic at 14px. For body, specimen-test three characterful OFL faces with confirmed smcp/c2sc/onum/tnum and pick by eye, not by table: Vollkorn (Althausen — genuinely underused in this genre, warm without being cream), Alegreya (Huerta Tipográfica — restless, calligraphic, full OT set), Piazzolla (Huerta Tipográfica — variable, Palatino-adjacent, slightly awkward in a way that reads as engineered). For display only, Fraunces at high opsz with WONK=1 gives the masthead a face literally nobody else in academic web has. For mono, Martian Mono (Evil Martians, variable width axis) over Plex — the condensed widths earn their keep in a 7rem rail and it has an actual face; keep Plex as the fallback only if the width axis fights the subsetter.

issues.problem: 'The site's ONE deliberate asymmetry' is a 7rem rail + 34rem text + 1fr — Tufte's layout, mirrored, present in every documentation site built since 2015 — and §4.3 states it collapses to a single column below 1100px. Audience 1 is described as the largest by a distance and arrives from a WhatsApp forward, i.e. on a 390px phone. The single signature layout move is therefore absent for the majority of visitors and for the priority audience. Mobile gets one sentence per page in §6 and is a plain single-column stack: the generic version of the site is the version most people see.
issues.fix: The rail must survive to 390px in a reduced form. Below 1100px keep a 2.75rem left rail carrying stage ticks — short 1px marks at each year, with the year set in Martian Mono condensed at 11px — so the left edge of every dated list still reads as a gauge axis at phone width. Spec mobile first for /, /publications/, /group/ and /join/ as full drawn layouts in §6, not as collapse notes. Then re-run test 16 on the 390px screenshot, not the 1440px one.

issues.problem: The best idea in the document is that the two interface colours are the wet and dry poles of one AR6 gradient, so interface and figures share a scientific palette. It is then capped at ~2% of painted pixels, and --mark (#8C5A24, the dry pole) is given 'exactly one job': the ↗ glyph on outbound links, with 'more than one per screen is a bug'. The system exists only in the colophon. A viewer sees off-white, near-black, and a tasteful dark teal — which is indistinguishable from every studio site of the last three years.
issues.fix: Put the gradient in 100% of painted pixels instead of 2%. Set --ink to #0F2621 rather than neutral #15191A — the entire site is written in the wet pole, so links at #166157 read as a lighter member of the same family rather than 'grey text plus a brand colour'. Then promote --mark #8C5A24 to a structural role that is his actual thesis: the dry pole means absence. Missing data, no open dataset, no self-hostable PDF, an unfunded project, a gap year in a record — all marked in #8C5A24. His whole argument is 'the gap is not in the models, it is in the observations'; make missing data have a colour on this site and the palette becomes a position instead of a swatch.

issues.problem: The one object on this site that no template could ever have — a hydrograph traced from his own discharge record — is specified as a full-bleed band at 8% opacity behind the masthead, a divider, and a footer glyph. At 8% opacity it is wallpaper: a decorative squiggle behind a hero, which is the generic move it was meant to replace. Three crops of one geometry is a logo treatment, not a design idea.
issues.fix: Draw it at full ink weight, at real size, as content. A 74rem × 140px hydrograph strip sitting directly under the masthead rule, with a real x-axis, real y-axis, and a mono caption: MUSI AT CHADERGHAT · 13–15 OCT 2020 · PEAK [value] m³/s. Run the flood-stage threshold as a horizontal 1px --ink rule that continues past the chart and becomes the page's first section hairline — the ornament is now the rule system. Then add the move nobody expects: draw the 1908 Musi flood peak as a dashed datum line above the 2020 trace, labelled, with the 2020 event visibly failing to reach it. That single line carries the city's whole hydrological history, is unGoogleable by a template, and gives the masthead an argument.

issues.problem: A 7/5 split with headline + lead + meta strip on the left and a captioned portrait on the right is the second-most-common personal-site hero in existence — better than centred, but only just. Below the fold it becomes a vertical stack of equal-width full-bleed bands separated by identical hairlines, then a 2×2 card grid of figure + headline + two sentences + a count. The brief grep-bans repeat(3, 1fr) and then specifies a features grid with four cells instead of three. There is no moment where the page breaks its own grid, no tension, no change of rhythm.
issues.fix: Three moves. (1) Give the page two rhythms, not one: prose stays at 34rem, but the publication list, the news rail and the alumni table run at 46rem, and the hydrograph strip and the group photograph bleed to the viewport edge past the 74rem container — so the page visibly widens and narrows as its content changes register. (2) Kill the 2×2 research grid. Render the four claims as four numbered sentences at lead size (21px), each on its own hairline, with the figure thumbnail in the right rail and a forecast-style metadata line in mono: CLAIM 01 · CONFIDENCE: HIGH · 11 PAPERS · REVISED 2026-03. Putting a confidence tag on his own claims is on-thesis ('say the uncertainty'), unusual, and impossible to template. (3) Break the grid once, deliberately: the group photograph runs full-bleed and uncropped, corridor and fluorescent tubes included.

issues.problem: The brief says 'keep his sentence rhythm', quotes his idiosyncratic article usage ('after masters at the IIT Kanpur'), and then writes three paragraphs of flawless standard editorial English containing none of it. Worse, both samples close on the short-declarative reversal that is the most detectable LLM cadence currently in circulation: 'The answer, repeatedly, is that the gap is not in the models. It is in the observations.' and 'Six papers, one app, one dashboard, and two PhD theses so far. It is not finished.' The banned-words list catches the 2023 tells (leverage, unlock, tapestry) and none of the 2026 ones. The client's number-one requirement is failing inside the brief's own showcase copy.
issues.fix: Add to the CI ban list, as regex not vocabulary: the reversal pattern /\b(is|was|are|were) not [^.]{3,60}\.\s+(It|They|That) (is|was|are|were)\b/; sentence-fragment paragraph closers under five words; more than one em-dash per paragraph; the words quiet, considered, deliberate, honest, actually, simply, real (as an intensifier); and any three-item list used as a cadence device ('the models, the apps, the dashboards'). Then rewrite both samples from a recording: interview him for twenty minutes, transcribe, and build the paragraphs from his actual clauses — keep at least two non-idiomatic constructions per page verbatim and put a note in the style guide that a copy-editor must not remove them. The headline 'I forecast floods.' also breaks the brief's own hard rule that every sentence carries a proper noun, a number, or a date — replace it with the fact only he can say: 'For seven years I forecast rivers across the continental United States. Since 2017, one city: Hyderabad.'

issues.problem: Twenty-six rows of computed contrast ratios across two tables, forty lines of tokens, a special-case exemption to the site's own zero-shadow policy ('shadows are invisible on #121614'), a permanent light plate so figures never invert — and not one sentence anywhere in the brief saying what dark mode is FOR or who uses it. The concept is paper: cool stock, hairlines, real small caps, tabular figures, a print stylesheet printed and read. A dark mode is a direct contradiction of that concept, and the design's own content refuses it. The ratio of rigour to intent here is the whole problem in miniature.
issues.fix: Pick a position and defend it. Either (a) ship light-only and say so in the colophon in one line — 'This site is a paper object. It does not have a dark mode.' — which is itself a point of view and costs forty lines less code; or (b) make dark mode a genuinely different design rather than swapped variables: dark = the forecast desk at night. Ground #0E1412, ink #D7DEDA, the hydrograph strip rendered as a live glowing trace, and the NWS stage-category colours (action #FFDC00, minor #FF9500, moderate #E8112D, major #7B1FA2) switched on for status elements only in this mode. Two registers the subject actually has — field notebook by day, operational console by night — instead of one design with its brightness inverted.

issues.problem: Three ink values where --ink-2 (6.17:1) and --ink-3 (5.15:1) are one point of contrast apart and visually identical in use. That is a ramp filled out because ramps have three steps — the exact signature of a generated token set. Similarly --r-1: 2px and --r-2: 3px are two radii no human can distinguish, existing only because 'forms need a little radius'.
issues.fix: Two inks: --ink #0F2621 and --ink-mute at 4.6:1. If a third tier is genuinely needed it must be far away — around 3.2:1, clearly a different class of information, used only for the gauge-rail years. One radius: 0, everywhere, inputs and chips included. A 0-radius text input on a 1px --rule-strong border is more distinctive than a 3px one and matches the print concept exactly.

issues.problem: #F7F8F6 is described as 'cool paper stock, deliberately not cream'. It is R246 G248 B246: a neutral near-white with a two-point green cast that no viewer will ever perceive on any display. The distinction from cream exists in the document and nowhere on screen. So the ground is off-white with one accent, which is the default the brief spends a page rejecting.
issues.fix: Commit at a value people can see and invert the default figure/ground relationship: ground --paper #E7EDE8 (a visibly tinted cool grey-green, still 13:1 against #0F2621 ink), with figure plates and the publication-detail pages at #FCFDFC. The page is tinted; the plates are the white. Every academic site is white with grey cards — this is the reverse, it is one token change, and it is legible at a glance from across a room.

issues.problem: Audited honestly: the gauge rail is Jeff Heer's .margin rule with the pixel value changed (the brief says so) and is standard in every Hugo academic theme; sidenotes are the Tufte CSS checkbox pattern, the single most-copied academic-web move of the last decade ('no competing site in Indian hydrology has this' is a very low bar); small-caps venue names are in every well-made CV since 1990; light figure plates are correct engineering with zero visual signature; a colophon is now itself a genre convention. Two of eight are actually his — the stage mark and the trainee marks — and one of those is set at 8% opacity. The section is a list of genre competencies labelled as a fingerprint.
issues.fix: Stop calling conventions fingerprints and add three details that only this site can have. (1) Build-time page numbers in the footer as if it were a printed bulletin — 'p. 14 of 61', computed across the sitemap. (2) Hovering a year in the publications rail rules a full-width hairline across the page at that year — a datum line, six lines of CSS, one of your two motion effects, and memorable. (3) A masthead 'issue' stamp: SATISHREGONDA.IN · ISSUE 47 · 4 SEP 2026, incremented per deploy — the site is a serial publication, which is true and which no template does.

issues.problem: '82% saturation, one grade' is the single most generic direction available; every editorial brief says desaturate slightly. Shot 1 is 'a Deccan river or reservoir at low sun' — the golden-hour landscape, i.e. stock. This on a site whose entire subject is monsoon: intense, short, badly-observed bursts of rain under flat grey cloud.
issues.fix: Ban golden hour on this site in writing. Shoot the whole set under monsoon overcast at 1–3pm, plus one night frame with direct phone flash on wet asphalt. Grade to the flat, slightly green cast of a survey photograph rather than to a warm editorial preset — no lifted blacks. And add the image system the project already owns: a tiled grid of real SnapFlood citizen submissions (with permission), each stamped with its timestamp and coordinates in mono beneath it, running full-bleed on /tools/snapflood/ and as the /group/ header. Ugly phone photographs of flooded streets are the visual language of the work, and they are the archive whose absence is his thesis.

issues.problem: An --accent-tint filled rounded box with an arrow link is a callout box, present on essentially every site built since 2018 — and it directly contradicts §4.2's own hard rule that --accent may 'never [be] a filled area, never a card background'. The most important element for the most important audience is rendered in the most generic component in the document.
issues.fix: No fill. A wire-service status line, full width, rules top and bottom at 1px --ink, set in Martian Mono caps: STATUS · 04 SEP 2026 · ACCEPTING PhD APPLICANTS FOR JAN 2027 · CLOSES 15 NOV · → HOW TO APPLY. It survives unchanged at 390px, it obeys the accent budget, it is unmistakably an operational bulletin rather than a marketing callout, and it reads as urgent because it looks like a product, not a promotion.

issues.problem: Thirteen rows, thirteen distinct sizes, several derived to a quarter-pixel (1.0313rem, 1.1875rem). The x-height matching is genuinely good rigour, but a thirteen-step scale is a system, not a voice — and the masthead at 52px is the timid middle: too big to be quiet, too small to be a statement, and on a bulletin nobody's name is set at 52px anyway.
issues.fix: Collapse to seven steps and make one of them a decision you cannot defend. The strongest option is contrarian and on-concept: set his name at 20px in mono caps in the masthead — the same weight as a document header — and let the hydrograph strip be the actual hero at full width. The first line of prose is then the largest type on the page at 21px. That is a page that says 'the data is the subject, not the man', which is both true of him and something no portfolio template would ever do.

issues.problem: '~2% of painted pixels' is presented as a hard rule inside a rubric that claims items 1–11 are machine-checkable. It is not measurable by any grep, and no one will ever compute it. It is rigour-shaped language performing a rule rather than being one.
issues.fix: Replace with something countable and add it to the grep script: at most six accent-coloured elements per viewport at 1440×900, zero filled accent areas larger than 2rem², and exactly one --mark element per page. Then actually add it to §11 as item 11b with the selector list it checks.

issues.section: §3 / whole document — absence of undefendable choices
issues.problem: Every single decision in §3 and §4 is justified by a citation, a measurement, a contrast ratio, a licence clause, or a binary diff. That is a document engineered to survive a review, and it is exactly what a machine produces when asked to be non-generic: safe defaults arranged very neatly, each with a footnote. Taste is by definition the part that cannot be justified. There are zero unjustifiable choices here, which is why the result will read as assembled rather than authored.
issues.fix: Require three decisions with no defence and write them into §3 as such. Candidates: the entire /publications/ page set in Martian Mono, every line, because a publication list is a data table and he can live with it; the h1 on every interior page at 64px against a 26rem measure, which is objectively too large and looks great; the footer set upside-down-adjacent as a colophon block in 11px mono running the full 74rem. Pick three, state plainly in the brief that they are matters of taste and not up for justification, and defend them by showing the printed specimen instead of arguing.

issues.problem: 'NOAA/NWS 2006–13 · World Bank 2014–16 · Johns Hopkins 2015–16 · IIT Hyderabad 2017–' is a CV line dressed as a hero element — a breadcrumb of logos without logos. In tabular mono the overlapping 2014–16 / 2015–16 reads as a typo rather than as a life.
issues.fix: Either cut it (the bio already carries the arc) or render it as a real 1px timeline strip 74rem wide with the overlap visible as two bars stacked — the overlap is the interesting part, and drawn it becomes a small piece of data graphics consistent with the hydrograph rather than a list of employers.

issues.problem: The motion budget of two effects is correct and I would keep the discipline. But one of the two is spent on link-underline thickness at 140ms, which is the single most common 'tasteful' hover on the web — the budget is rigorous and the spend is generic.
issues.fix: Keep the underline transition as effect one but spend effect two on the datum-line hover described above: hovering any year in the gauge rail draws a 1px --rule hairline across the full viewport width at that baseline, 120ms. CSS-only, on-concept, and it is the kind of thing a visitor mentions to someone else.

issues.problem: Address, email, four profile links, RSS, colophon, 'Last updated 14 September 2026'. This is the default academic footer and the last thing on every page.
issues.fix: Make it the product footer of a bulletin: ISSUING OFFICE Room B-212, Dept of Civil Engineering, IIT Hyderabad, Kandi 502284 · NEXT SCHEDULED UPDATE 0130 IST DAILY · ISSUE 47 · BUILD a3f91c · p. 14 of 61. Same information, one unmistakable voice, zero extra work given the build already knows all of it.

issues.problem: 'Research · Publications · Tools · Group · Teaching · Writing' is the default academic nav in the default order. Nav is where a point of view is cheapest, and this spends nothing.
issues.fix: Keep the routes, retitle two: Tools → What you can use, Group → RAFT. And set the nav in mono at 13px with a leading index number (01–06) to match the bulletin register. Small, free, and the first thing a visitor reads stops sounding like a CMS.

issues.problem: '3 quotable lines' pre-written for journalists is the most press-release element in a document whose §2 forbids sounding like a press release, on a site whose stated copy value is to state uncertainty.
issues.fix: Replace with three things he has actually said, pulled verbatim from the 2023 NewsMeter / Hans India / Deccan Chronicle pieces, each with outlet and date attached. Journalists want a sourced prior quote more than a fresh canned one, and it costs no writing.

missing: EVENT MODE — the single biggest missed opportunity in the document. Audience 4 is described as time-critical with traffic spiking during monsoon and flood events, and the site as designed is identical on a dry Tuesday and during a Musi flood. Add a three-state site condition (NORMAL / WATCH / EVENT) driven by one Settings cell plus a scheduled rebuild: in EVENT the home page swaps to a bulletin — the hydrograph strip goes live-adjacent, an NWS-style stage-category band appears at the top, the recruiting line drops below the fold, and /tools/snapflood/ and the press contact rise to the top. It serves the audience the brief says is unreachable, it is impossible for any template to have, and it makes the whole 'operational forecast bulletin' concept true instead of asserted.

ANY Indian or local visual reference at all. §3 explicitly exiles the Indian signal to 'the content, the accent's provenance and the Telugu outreach page' and then it never appears in the design. The 1908 Musi flood — the event that produced Osman Sagar and Himayat Sagar and Visvesvaraya's plan, and the reason Hyderabad's drainage is what it is — is the most resonant fact available to this site and appears nowhere in the brief. It belongs on the masthead hydrograph as a dashed historical datum line, and in one 40-word footnote on /research/urban-flooding-hyderabad/.

A TYPE SPECIMEN AS A DELIVERABLE. Phase 2 produces tokens.css and a component set — a spec table, not a proof. Add: before any code, print an A3 specimen at 100% showing one publication entry, one news line, one alumni row, the masthead, and one full prose paragraph; kill it and reset it three times; pin the survivor to a wall and choose by eye. No brief that has never been printed can claim print-trained typography.
A DEFINITION OF WHAT DARK MODE IS FOR. Two contrast tables, forty tokens, a policy exemption, and zero sentences of intent.

MOBILE AS A DESIGNED ARTEFACT. Every layout in §6 is drawn at desktop with one collapse sentence appended. The priority audience arrives on a phone from a WhatsApp forward. Draw /, /publications/, /group/ and /join/ at 390px as full specs, and re-run rubric item 16 (the 20px blur test) on the mobile screenshot.

404, EMPTY AND ERROR STATES. /404 is listed as 'Generated'. The 404 page, an empty search result, a tool that is offline, and an alumni row with no placement yet are the four places a site reveals whether a person made it. Design all four — the 404 as a bulletin reading NO PRODUCT ISSUED FOR THIS LOCATION, with the site's index below it, is free and correct.

A CI RULE AGAINST THE CURRENT-GENERATION PROSE CADENCE. §2's banned list catches 2023 vocabulary and misses the 2026 rhythm, which is what actually reads as machine-written — and which appears in the brief's own sample copy. Regex the patterns, not just the words.

AN EXPLICIT LIST OF WHAT THIS SITE DOES THAT NONE OF THE EIGHT REFERENCE SITES DO. The reference table has a 'What we take' column and no 'What we refuse' column. Write the second column. If it comes out short, the direction is a collage and needs another pass before anyone writes CSS.

lens: Two-year maintainability by a non-technical owner after the developer is gone — every step of the editing workflow, and the total count of moving parts
verdict: The brief contains one genuinely rare and correct longevity decision — step ⑤, committing fetched JSON and rendered Markdown back into the repo, so the site rebuilds with no network and survives Google entirely. That single choice puts this ahead of most "client edits a Sheet" designs I have watched die. Everything built around it, however, is all-or-nothing, desktop-only, and quietly dependent on a developer who by hypothesis does not exist. A half-typed publication row freezes every unrelated edit including the recruiting notice; the "🌐 Website → 🚀 Publish now" button does not exist in the Google Sheets mobile app, so the single most time-sensitive edit on the site cannot be made from an airport; the escape-hatch table in §9 says "Developer" eight times and names nobody; and the CI style rubric — banned words, grep checks — is wired to block *his* content publishes, meaning the word "robust" in a hydrology blog post takes the site's build down. The publications automation will not survive contact: §9 promises student authorship is marked automatically, §7.4 requires him to hand-type positional indices (`0:phd; 1:phd`) per paper, and an OpenAlex-seeded PR reviewed on GitHub by a professor with no GitHub habit will produce one wrong author list — a co-PI marked as a PhD student — and then be abandoned. It is also roughly thirty named components, six of them bespoke and unmaintained on handover day (the Sheets loader, the Docs-zip sanitiser, the unescape pass, the WeasyPrint CV, Satori OG cards, the fontTools subsetting step); an MVP with about nine parts delivers 80% of the value. Fix the twelve items below marked blocker and major and this survives two years. Ship it as written and it degrades to a site nobody dares press the button on, which is how these die: not with a crash, but with an owner who stops trying.

issues.problem: The build is all-or-nothing. One incomplete row — he starts a publication at 4pm, gets pulled into a meeting, leaves `venue` blank — makes the whole build fail, and the site is frozen for every other edit until that row is fixed. This is exactly the 11pm-before-a-grant-deadline scenario: he needs to change one sentence in `recruiting_status` and cannot, because a student's photo was deleted from Drive last week. "Nothing on the website has changed" is reassuring the first time and infuriating the fifth.
issues.fix: Split validation into fatal and skippable. Fatal (build stops, site unchanged): missing tab, missing header column, `Settings` unreadable. Everything else — a bad row in Publications, People, News, Photos, Tools — is SKIPPED with a warning and the rest publishes. The skipped row is reported in three places: the `_Publish Log` line (`⚠️ Published with 1 item skipped — Publications row 12: 'year' says "forthcoming"`), the email, and a noindex `/_status/` page he can bookmark. Add a `Status` column to each tab with a formula that shows ⚠️ next to any row missing a required field, so he sees it in the sheet before he ever presses the button.

issues.problem: Apps Script custom menus do not render in the Google Sheets iOS or Android app. The "🌐 Website → 🚀 Publish now" menu is desktop-only. The highest-frequency, most time-sensitive edit on the entire site — the dated recruiting status, and the `currently` block — is the one he will most often want to change from a phone at a conference or in an airport. The brief's answer to "on his phone" is Sveltia at `/admin`, which requires him to have a GitHub fine-grained PAT in his password manager. He will not.
issues.fix: Verify on a phone in five minutes before writing any code. Then replace the menu as the primary trigger with a checkbox: `Settings!publish_now`, watched by an INSTALLABLE `onEdit` trigger (these do fire for edits made in the mobile app, unlike simple triggers and unlike custom menus). The trigger unticks the box, dispatches, and toasts. Keep the desktop menu as a convenience alias to the same function. Reframe Sveltia in the documentation as a developer's recovery tool, not something he is ever expected to use — or cut it (see the MVP issue).

issues.problem: These two sections contradict each other. §9 promises "any paper they co-author is marked automatically" once a student is added to `People`. §7.4 defines `author_marks` as hand-typed positional pairs (`0:phd; 1:phd`) on every publication row. Positional indices are the worst possible encoding here: if an author is added, removed, or reordered — including by the OpenAlex bot — the marks silently shift and attach to the wrong person. Marking a senior co-PI as a PhD student is a professional insult, it is invisible in a diff, and it is the exact defect that gets a feature quietly abandoned. It also guarantees signature detail #3 (the trainee legend, one of the site's stated fingerprints) is empty in practice, because nobody maintains positional indices across 39 rows.
issues.fix: Delete the `author_marks` column. Add an `aliases` column to `People` (`Ponukumati, P.; P. Ponukumati; Padmini Ponukumati`). At build time, mark any author string in a publication that matches a `People.name` or alias, using that person's `role` and their `start_year`/`end_year` to pick the mark. Adding a student to `People` then retroactively marks every paper, which is what §9 already promises. Print unmatched-but-close author strings in the publish log as `⚠️ 'Mohammed, A.' looks like a group member but is not in People` so the mapping self-corrects.

issues.problem: The automation as specified will produce a wrong author list within the first quarter. OpenAlex's ORCID filter resolves to its own author *entity*, not to per-work ORCID assertions (the brief's own recon proves this — Crossref-by-ORCID returns 5 works, OpenAlex returns 55), so it inherits OpenAlex's disambiguation errors: merged authors, initials-only author strings from AMS and Elsevier metadata, book chapters whose `venue` is the book. The review gate is "opens a pull request" — a professor with no GitHub habit will not review a diff of author strings two years from now. He will merge it, or ignore it until the PR list is 30 deep.
issues.fix: Keep the query, change the destination and the scope. The bot writes ONLY `doi`, `year`, `title` and a `source_url` — never `authors`, never `venue`, never marks — into a new `Inbox` tab in the Sheet, highlighted, with a one-line note: "New paper found. Check it, fill in authors and venue, then cut the row into Publications." No GitHub PR, no merge, no account he does not use. He types the author list himself, once, correctly, in the form he wants it cited. If that is too much friction, cut the automation entirely for v1 — three new papers a year is a ten-minute annual task, not a system worth thirty lines of dedupe logic.

issues.section: §9 "What you cannot do yourself" / §8.5 last row
issues.problem: The escape-hatch table lists "Developer" eight times and the failure table's answer to "the developer is unreachable" is a RUNBOOK in a private GitHub repo he cannot open, plus "a named IITH second owner" who is still an open question (§12.14) rather than a launch gate. Meanwhile the GitHub workflow-failure email in §8.2 ⑧ goes to the developer's watched-repo subscription — an account that may not exist in two years. So the design's primary error channel dies with the developer.
issues.fix: Three changes. (1) Make the failure email originate from HIM: an Apps Script time-driven trigger (every 15 minutes) reads the newest `_Publish Log` row and, if it is ❌ or ⚠️, sends a plain-English MailApp email to him and to the named second owner. Sent from his own account, so it can never be blocked, filtered as spoofed, or depend on anyone's GitHub subscription. (2) The runbook is a Google Doc in `/Website/`, plus a printed page in his desk drawer, plus a copy in the repo — and the 10-minute screen recording is an MP4 in Drive, not a hosted link. (3) Make "second owner named, added to Cloudflare + GitHub + the GCP project, and recovery codes stored somewhere he controls" a Phase 0 checkbox, not open question 14.

issues.problem: Roughly thirty named components, six of them bespoke code with no upstream maintainer: the custom Sheets Content Layer loader, the Docs `text/markdown` unescape pass, the `application/zip` HTML sanitiser behind a flag, WeasyPrint (a Python toolchain inside a JS build) for the CV PDF, Satori/resvg OG generation, and the fontTools subsetting step. Every one of those is a thing that breaks silently and cannot be fixed by anyone but the author. The 17-day estimate is optimistic by roughly 2× on Phases 3 and 4, and the parts that get cut when a schedule slips are always the pipeline-robustness parts — leaving precisely the fragile version.
issues.fix: Ship the MVP: Cloudflare Pages + DNS, one GitHub repo, one Sheet, one Drive Docs folder, one read-only service account, one Apps Script publish trigger, Astro, committed Markdown-with-frontmatter, one static OG image. Nine parts. Cut for v1 and revisit only if he asks: WeasyPrint (the CV page uses the print stylesheet you are already building in Phase 2 — 'Print → Save as PDF'; or link the PDF CV he already maintains); Satori/resvg (one static OG card site-wide); Pagefind (twenty pages and 39 publications do not need a search index — the filter chips plus Ctrl-F cover it); Sveltia; MathML prerendering (nothing in the sitemap has math); the OpenAlex bot; the `Manual`, `Talks` and `Awards` tabs until there is content for them. Move the fontTools subsetting OUT of the pipeline: run it once, commit the four .woff2 files, delete the script from CI. Every one of these is additive later; none is load-bearing for the audience analysis in §1.

issues.problem: The most common way a site like this dies in year two is not in the brief at all: the domain expires. There is no line about auto-renew, no named registrar account owner, no card-on-file expiry, no calendar reminder, and no inventory of who owns each account (registrar, Cloudflare, GitHub, GCP, and the Drive folder itself — which, if it sits in the developer's personal Google account, vanishes on handover). §12.1 asks whether the domain is even registered but never asks who controls the renewal.
issues.fix: Add to Phase 0, as blocking checkboxes: domain auto-renew ON with a card that does not expire before 2030; registrar account owned by him or IITH with the developer added as a secondary, never the reverse; the GCP project created under an account he owns; the Drive folder owned by his IITH account, not the developer's; a one-page `ACCOUNTS.md` (also a Google Doc, also printed) listing every account, its owner, its recovery path and its renewal date; and calendar reminders in HIS calendar 60 days before the domain and any card expiry. Also add a restore test to Phase 6: a second person clones the repo on a clean machine with no Google credentials and rebuilds the site. If that has never been done, the escape hatch is a claim, not a feature.

issues.problem: No concurrency control anywhere. He presses Publish now, sees nothing happen for 30 seconds, presses it again. Two `repository_dispatch` events, two builds, both committing fetched JSON to the same branch: the second push fails non-fast-forward, or both deploy and the slower-but-older build wins, silently publishing stale content over fresh. This is also the literal answer to "what happens when two people edit at once" — the sheet handles simultaneous edits fine, but the publish path does not.
issues.fix: Three lines. (1) `concurrency: {group: publish, cancel-in-progress: true}` on the build job. (2) `git pull --rebase` before the content push, and fail loudly if the rebase conflicts. (3) In Apps Script, take a `LockService` script lock and check the newest `_Publish Log` timestamp: if a publish started less than three minutes ago, toast "A publish is already running — your changes are included in it" and do not dispatch. He gets a truthful message instead of a silent double-fire.

issues.section: §11 Anti-generic rubric enforced in CI / §2 banned words
issues.problem: The style rubric is wired as a build gate on the same pipeline that publishes his content. So: he writes a blog post using "robust" — a standard technical term in his own field (robust regression, robustness of an ensemble) — and CI fails his publish and emails him that a word is banned. A house-style rule has become a production outage aimed at the site's owner, and the first time it happens he learns that the button is unsafe. That is precisely the moment these systems get abandoned.
issues.fix: Split CI into two jobs with different powers. `content-publish` (triggered by him) runs headers, Zod, images, build, deploy — and reports style violations as warnings in the log only, never a failure. `code-pr` (triggered by a developer's pull request) runs the full anti-generic rubric, the grep script, budget.json, lychee and gitleaks as hard gates. Also drop `robust` from the banned list entirely, and scope the banned-word check to developer-authored template copy, not to prose he wrote.

issues.problem: The single most frequently edited tab — recruiting status, `currently`, phone, all the profile URLs — is stored as one horizontal row under a header row. It is the layout most vulnerable to exactly what a non-technical user does: inserting a row above it, sorting, or a column being added in the wrong place. Any of those shifts every value one cell over, and the build either fails or silently publishes the department name into the email field.
issues.fix: Make `Settings` a two-column key/value tab: column A `key`, column B `value`, read by key lookup. Immune to row order, immune to column insertion, immune to sorting. It also reads better on a phone, where the horizontal-row layout requires scrolling right past twenty columns to reach `recruiting_status`. Put `recruiting_status`, `recruiting_deadline` and `currently` in the top three rows so they are the first thing on screen.

issues.problem: `slug` and `id` are marked "frozen" but a spreadsheet cannot enforce that, and nothing describes what happens when he edits one or deletes a row. Both are silent URL destruction: `/publications/2023-imerg-hyderabad/` 404s, Google Scholar de-indexes the paper, and every citation link anyone saved breaks. The brief correctly provides an `exclude` checkbox but never tells him to use it instead of deleting, and never enforces it.
issues.fix: Diff against the committed previous JSON on every build. If an `id` changed, auto-emit `old → new 301` into `_redirects` and log it — forgive, do not block. If an `id` disappeared without `exclude` ticked, keep serving the old page, add a `noindex` tombstone, and warn: "Publication 2023-imerg-hyderabad was removed from the sheet. Its page is still live so citation links keep working. Tick 'exclude' instead of deleting rows." Store `slug_history` in the committed JSON. Put "Never delete a row — tick `exclude`" in the row-1 cell note and in the README tab.

issues.problem: The instruction is "right-click → Share → Copy link" and paste the URL into `photo`. This fails in the two most likely real cases and the failure table covers neither: (a) the file is not inside `/Website/Images/` — he saved it to Drive root from his phone, or a student emailed it — so the service account gets 403 and the build fails on a file he can see perfectly well in his own browser; (b) the file's sharing is Restricted and the copied link works for him because he owns it. "Build fails naming the file" is not actionable when the message is a permissions error on a file he is looking at.
issues.fix: Stop accepting URLs. Add an Apps Script sidebar or menu item "Insert a photo" that lists the files in `/Website/Images/` and writes the chosen filename into the cell — he picks from a list, never pastes a link. As a belt-and-braces fallback, have the Apps Script publish trigger (which runs as HIM, with full Drive access) pre-flight every Drive reference before dispatching: if the file exists but is outside `/Website/Images/`, MOVE it there automatically and carry on; if it does not exist, refuse to dispatch and say which cell, in a dialog, in the sheet, before any build runs. Client-side beats build-time here for the same reason the brief already argues for the ✅/❌ formulas.

issues.problem: Three problems in one workflow. (1) Fixing a typo in a published post is never described: he edits the Doc and nothing happens, because publishing is triggered from the spreadsheet, a different app. He will edit it again, then conclude it is broken. (2) "Drag the document into `Published/`" does not work well in the Drive mobile app and breaks entirely if the Doc has been added to two folders or accessed via a shortcut. (3) There is no version pinning — a half-finished edit at 11pm goes live at the nightly build.
issues.fix: Replace folder-as-state with a `Status` row in the settings table the Doc already carries: `draft` / `published` / `retired`. One place, visible inside the document he is editing, works on any device, no dragging. Add one sentence to the workflow: "After you edit a published post, go to the spreadsheet and press Publish now — or wait for the nightly update." Run the cron twice daily rather than nightly so "wait" means hours, not a day. And keep the last successfully-rendered Markdown for each post committed in the repo, so a mid-edit Doc or a changed export format cannot replace good prose with garbage.

issues.section: §8.3 Secrets / §9 "Rotate the Google access key (once a year)"
issues.problem: An annual key rotation is a ritual assigned to a person who will not be there, and it creates a failure mode (the rotation that never happens, or the rotation that breaks the build) against an essentially nonexistent threat: a read-only credential scoped to one spreadsheet whose contents are published on a public website. Separately, the brief does not address that many Google Workspace orgs now block service-account key creation by policy, or that a project sitting in the developer's personal Google account disappears on handover.
issues.fix: Delete the annual rotation from the maintenance list; document the key's existence and its recovery path in the runbook instead, and rotate only on handover or compromise. Add a build step that reads the key's `valid_before` if one is set and warns 30 days out. Create the GCP project under an account HE owns, with the developer as an added owner. And add a documented dead-Google mode: an environment variable `SHEETS_DISABLED=1` in the Cloudflare dashboard makes the build serve the committed content and deploy anyway — one toggle any competent person can flip over a phone call, turning the brief's best decision into something actually reachable under pressure.

issues.problem: The repo is private (Phase 0) and GitHub Actions is used for the PR gates, the weekly OpenAlex job, and the failure notification. Private repos get 2,000 free Actions minutes a month, and when they run out Actions stop silently at the account level — including, in this design, the error-reporting path. So the failure mode of "free minutes ran out" is "publishes stop working and nobody is told."
issues.fix: Make the repo public. There are no secrets in it — credentials live in CI — and the content is a public website. Public gets unlimited Actions minutes, gives GitHub Pages as a free hosting fallback if Cloudflare ever becomes a problem, and materially improves longevity because anyone can clone and rebuild. Keep drafts in Drive, where they already are. If he objects to a public repo, then move every recurring job to Cloudflare Workers Builds and make the failure email come from Apps Script (see the developer-unreachable fix), so no notification path depends on Actions minutes.

issues.problem: Two bespoke parsers against an undocumented export format — the `text/markdown` "unescape pass" and the `application/zip` HTML sanitiser behind a flag — are among the most likely things to break silently, and the mitigation offered is "flip a flag," which is a developer action. Google Docs will happily give him tables, columns, footnotes, drawings, smart chips and comments, none of which either parser handles predictably.
issues.fix: Constrain and reject rather than parse and hope. Define the allowed Doc vocabulary (headings, bold, italic, links, lists, blockquote, images with an italic caption line, plus the settings table) and have the build refuse the post with a friendly named message — "Your post 'Musi notes' contains a table on page 2. Tables are not supported; the post was not published, the rest of the site updated normally" — rather than mangling it. Under skip-and-warn, this costs him one post, never the site. Keep the last good rendered Markdown committed per post so a change in Google's export format degrades to stale-but-correct prose.

issues.problem: Three parts of the brief contradict each other. Cloudflare Web Analytics injects a beacon from `static.cloudflareinsights.com`; the stated CSP is `default-src 'none'` with `script-src 'self'`, which blocks it; and the performance budget mandates zero third-party requests on every page type. As written, either analytics silently does not work or the CSP and the budget are wrong.
issues.fix: Use Cloudflare zone-level analytics from the dashboard, which requires no page code, no beacon, no cookie and no consent notice. The CSP, the budget and the zero-third-party claim all stay true, and he still gets traffic numbers he will look at twice a year.

issues.problem: There is no ordering anywhere in the publication display. Within a year the order is presumably sheet-row order, which is never stated; and `selected` is a boolean with a "max 8 TRUE" rule that a spreadsheet cannot enforce and that gives no control over which six appear first on the home page. He will want his own first-author paper at the top of 2026, and there is no way to do it.
issues.fix: Add `selected_order` (int, blank = fall back to year). State in the README tab: "Within a year, papers appear in the order of the rows — drag a row to move it, or use Data → Sort range." Put a live count in the header cell (`Selected: 6 / 8`) with conditional formatting turning red above 8, and have the build take the first eight by order with a warning rather than failing.

issues.problem: A nag email is the weakest possible mechanism, and a stale dated recruiting notice is actively harmful — the brief makes exactly this argument about blogs. "Accepting PhD students for the January 2027 intake, apply by 15 November" still sitting on the home page in March 2027 tells the site's largest audience that nobody maintains this site.
issues.fix: Make the block self-degrading, not nagging. Render it with a visible provenance line from day one ("Status as of 4 September 2026"). After `recruiting_deadline` passes, automatically swap to a neutral, permanently-true line — "Admissions run through the IIT Hyderabad portal; write to me if you are interested" — with a link to `/join/`. Keep the warning email as a secondary prompt. The page must never be able to state something false without him doing anything.

issues.problem: If the derivative images (AVIF/WebP/JPEG at three widths, content-hashed) are committed alongside the JSON, the repo grows monotonically and never garbage-collects — every re-crop of the group photo adds nine new files and orphans nine old ones. Over two years of photographs and blog images this becomes a slow, invisible problem in the one artefact that is supposed to be the permanent record.
issues.fix: Commit the ORIGINALS downloaded from Drive (one file each, the true source of record) and treat derivatives as build output cached in Workers Builds, regenerated on demand. If you keep derivatives in the repo for offline-rebuild purity, add a prune step in the same job that deletes any hashed file no longer referenced by the built site.

issues.problem: A bespoke escape-hatch command that nobody ever runs is a command that does not work when it is finally needed. It will bit-rot within a year of the last commit, and by definition it is only invoked when the person who could fix it is unavailable.
issues.fix: Delete it. Commit content as Markdown-with-frontmatter rather than JSON at step ⑤, and the eject path becomes `git clone` — the content is already in the format any static site generator on earth can read. That is a strictly stronger guarantee than a script, and it removes a part.

issues.problem: Cloudflare Email Routing forwards mail, and forwarded mail regularly fails SPF/DKIM alignment at the receiving end. If a `hello@satishregonda.in` alias is the address printed on the press page and IITH's filter silently quarantines forwarded mail, journalist enquiries during a monsoon event vanish with no bounce. Audience 4 is described as time-critical.
issues.fix: Publish `satishr@ce.iith.ac.in` directly as the primary contact everywhere — it is already public on the IITH directory, so nothing is protected by hiding it. Use Email Routing only as an optional vanity alias, and add a Phase 6 checkbox: send a test message to the alias from an outside account and confirm it lands in his inbox, not his spam folder.

missing: Domain renewal and account ownership: auto-renew status, whose card is on file, when it expires, and calendar reminders in HIS calendar. The single most common cause of death for a site like this and it appears nowhere in the brief.

An ACCOUNTS inventory naming the owner and recovery path for every account: registrar, Cloudflare, GitHub, GCP project, the Drive folder itself, and the Play Store listing. Any of these sitting in the developer's personal Google account is a two-year time bomb.

A restore test in Phase 6: a second person clones the repo on a clean machine with no Google credentials and rebuilds the site successfully. Until that has been done, 'it rebuilds with no network access at all' is a claim, not a feature.

A handover acceptance test: he performs all eight workflows unaided while someone watches and takes notes — including one from a phone. Any task he cannot complete alone is a design defect, not a training gap.

Total annual cost of ownership in rupees: domain renewal, and an explicit statement that Cloudflare, GitHub, GCP and OpenAlex are all zero on the tiers used — plus what happens if any of those free tiers changes.
Spend and quota alerting on the Cloudflare and GCP accounts, so a surprise bill or a quota trip is noticed rather than discovered as an outage.

A stated policy on dependency updates. A frozen build that keeps working is the goal here, not a current one — so pin the Node version in .node-version, disable Dependabot except for security advisories on the toolchain, and say so in the runbook rather than leaving a repo that slowly accumulates unread PRs.
What happens if he moves institution, retires, or the group closes: who owns the domain and the content then, and whether the site is archived.

A one-page 'what to do when something is wrong' card for him, in Drive and printed, whose first line is 'the website is still showing the last good version, nothing is broken for visitors' — the reassurance that stops a panicked 11pm escalation.

lens: Completeness and internal consistency — what a builder hits on day one
verdict: The brief is exceptional on design rationale, failure modes and editor ergonomics, and it genuinely resolves the RAFT/raftwaters.in question (self-sufficient /group/, one build-time constant that renders nothing when empty, a documented refusal to link raftwaters.com — that is resolved, not hand-waved). But it is not buildable as written. It specifies six routes in layout detail out of twenty-plus, and the content model is missing the collections that even the specified pages depend on: there is no Education/Appointments/Service collection anywhere, yet the home trajectory strip, /about/ and the generated CV all render one, and the whole editorial spine (NOAA → World Bank → JHU → IITH) has no data source. Three load-bearing technical decisions contradict each other across sections: a read-only Viewer service account that must write the _Publish Log; a zero-third-party-request budget alongside Cloudflare Web Analytics and a CSP that blocks it; a Workers static-assets host deployed with the Pages command. Its own counts disagree in five places (39/55/56 publications, 15/18 alumni, 9/12 current students, 6/8 selected papers, 12/13 redirects), and the publication filter chips do not match the Research slugs they are validated against. Empty states are specified exactly where they were easy (RAFT link, Awards, missing student photo — that last one is genuinely well handled) and absent where they are likely (blog with zero posts, alumnus with no placement, paper with no abstract, no recruiting deadline set, /404 itself). The build plan inverts dependencies at its two highest-latency points: the photography that the home LCP and rubric item 17 depend on is scheduled after the page build, and the alumni placement round — which the brief itself calls the single highest-value content on the site and which requires reaching fifteen-to-eighteen people by WhatsApp — sits inside a two-day phase.

issues.problem: There is no Education, Appointments, or Service collection. /about/'s blocks are "Long bio → education → appointments → service", the home page renders a mono trajectory strip ("NOAA/NWS 2006–13 · World Bank 2014–16 · Johns Hopkins 2015–16 · IIT Hyderabad 2017–"), and §7.7 says the CV is "Built from Settings, Bio, Publications, Projects, People, Teaching, Talks, Awards". None of those hold an employment or degree record. The editorial spine of the entire site — the arc §2 calls verified fact — has no place it is edited.
issues.fix: Add a `Positions` tab (`kind` enum appointment/education/visiting · `org`✓ · `role`✓ · `city` · `start`✓ · `end` · `note` · `order`) and a `Service` tab (`kind` enum editorial/review/committee/membership · `body`✓ · `role`✓ · `start`✓ · `end`). Render Positions three ways: the home trajectory strip (kind=appointment, top 4 by order), /about/ education + appointments, and the CV. Service renders on /about/ and the CV, and the section is suppressed at zero rows the same way Awards is.

issues.problem: §8.3 says share every Sheet to the service account as **Viewer** with scope `spreadsheets.readonly`. §8.2 says the service account "has Editor on this ONE protected tab" and writes `_Publish Log`. Both cannot be true: Google Sheets range protections restrict editors, they never elevate a file-level Viewer, and `spreadsheets.readonly` cannot write any range. The publish-log feedback loop — the thing §9 teaches him to check after every publish — cannot run as specified.
issues.fix: Decide one: (a) the service account is a file-level **Editor** with `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets`, and every tab except `_Publish Log` is protected with the service account excluded — then say so in §8.3 and drop the "read-only service account" security claim; or (b) keep it read-only and write the log from the Apps Script (which already runs as him and already fires the dispatch), with the build reporting status back via a `repository_dispatch` callback or a GitHub Actions email only. (b) preserves the security posture and is one function.

issues.problem: Step ⑤ commits fetched JSON and rendered Markdown back into the repo, and Cloudflare Workers Builds trigger on push. As written every publish commits, which triggers a build, which commits again — an infinite build loop that will burn the 3,000 free minutes. Separately, the 01:17 cron, the Apps Script button and `workflow_dispatch` can all run at once; nothing serialises the commit-back, so two concurrent runs race on `git push` and one fails or clobbers.
issues.fix: Specify: the commit-back uses a bot author and `[skip ci]`, and Workers Builds is configured to ignore pushes authored by that bot; add GitHub Actions `concurrency: {group: publish, cancel-in-progress: false}` (or a repo-level lock) around the fetch/commit/deploy job; and make the commit a no-op when the fetched payload hash is unchanged, so the nightly cron produces no commit on a quiet day.

issues.problem: §8.4 mandates **0 third-party requests** on every page type and rubric item 10 makes it a launch blocker; §8.3 sets `script-src 'self'` with `default-src 'none'`. Cloudflare Web Analytics works by injecting a beacon script fetched from `static.cloudflareinsights.com` — a third-party request that the site's own CSP blocks. As specified, analytics silently does not work and the rubric item is unfalsifiable.
issues.fix: Drop the beacon. Use Cloudflare's server-side request analytics (zone/Workers analytics in the dashboard) which needs no script, no CSP exception and no consent notice, and state in §8.4 that the site ships no client-side analytics. If page-level detail is genuinely wanted later, it needs an explicit CSP `script-src` entry and a rewrite of the zero-third-party rule — say which.

issues.problem: The host is "Cloudflare Workers, static assets" but the deploy line is `wrangler pages deploy dist` — that is the Pages command and deploys to a different product. The mechanism for the §8.3 security headers and the §5 redirect table on Workers assets is never named. Worse, the redirect logic is wrong at the premise: the twelve mapped paths (`/home`, `/students`, `/raft`…) are paths on **sites.google.com**, and a redirect file on satishregonda.in never sees that traffic. The brief admits Google Sites permits no 301 and no canonical, then ships a redirect map as if it solved migration.
issues.fix: Pick the product and use its command (`wrangler deploy` with an assets binding, or commit to Pages and say so); name the file or Worker that emits `_headers`/`_redirects`. Then separate the two problems: (1) keep the map, relabelled "vanity paths on the new domain", and (2) add the actual migration lever — the stripped one-page Google Site with a visible link and a `<meta http-equiv=refresh>` to the matching new URL per retained page, plus a Search Console reconsideration note that no change-of-address is possible from Google Sites, plus the Phase 6 inbound-link updates already listed.

issues.problem: The Scholar-legal paper page is built on "Full author-written abstract, visible in the initial HTML. NEVER an accordion" — this is the single most detailed technical requirement in the brief. But §7.4 makes `abstract` optional and required only *if a PDF is set*, which is backwards; no phase sources 39 abstracts; and the rights question the brief carefully asks about PDFs (Open Q6) is never asked about abstracts, most of which are publisher copyright. Thirty-nine near-empty pages is also a thin-content problem for the site's own SEO.
issues.fix: Make `abstract` required for every row where `exclude` is FALSE, and add Phase 1 line items: pull abstracts from OpenAlex `abstract_inverted_index` and Crossref, flag every one whose source licence is unclear, and add to "from him": approval to reuse his own submitted abstracts (he is an author on all 39, which resolves most of it). Specify the fallback render for a paper with no abstract: title, authors, venue, DOI and a one-line `takeaway`, with `noindex` off but no empty ABSTRACT heading.

issues.problem: Phase 4 (Pages, 4 days) lists "From him: the field photographs … the three approved portraits … the group photograph" — but the photography is **Phase 5**, after it. The home page's above-the-fold LCP element is a field photograph; rubric item 17 ("every image a real photograph … zero stock") is a launch blocker; and the shoot depends on his travel, on students being on campus for a dated group photo, and on there being a wet Hyderabad street to photograph (item 4 on the shot list) — which is seasonal.
issues.fix: Move the shoot to Phase 0/1 and rename it "Phase 1b — Photography (his time, scheduled first)". Brief the shot list in the Phase 0 kickoff, book the group photo on a date when the group is assembled, and specify what Phase 4 builds against in the meantime (a labelled grey plate at the exact 4:5 aspect so no reflow occurs on swap). Flag shot 4 as monsoon-dependent with an archive fallback from his own group's existing field photos.

issues.problem: Alumni destinations are called "the single highest-value content on the entire site" and "the highest-value new content", and they require him to reach fifteen-to-eighteen former students by WhatsApp and get replies. That is a two-to-six week human latency, and it is buried in a two-day Phase 1 alongside DOI corrections. If it slips, the one thing that differentiates /group/ from every other lab page ships empty.
issues.fix: Move the alumni round to Phase 0, day one, as its own tracked item with a named owner. Give him a pre-written WhatsApp message and a Google Form that writes straight into the `People` tab (`first_position`, `sector`), so replies need no retyping. Set a hard cutoff date in the plan and specify the partial-ship render (see the empty-state issue below) so the page can launch at any completion level.

issues.problem: The budget rows do not sum to the stated totals: home is 15+14+20+148+100 = **297 KB** against a "Total first view ≤ 250 KB"; the publication page is 20+14+20+148+140 = **342 KB** against ≤ 300 KB. Separately, Pagefind is chosen in §8.1 but appears in no budget row, has no route in the sitemap, and no search UI in the masthead or footer layout — and the Pagefind runtime plus wasm alone exceeds the 20 KB JS budget before any index chunk loads.
issues.fix: Restate the totals as 300 KB (home) / 350 KB (publication page) with fonts counted, or drop a font cut to get under 250. Then either cut Pagefind (see the cut item) or give it a `/search/` route, a budget line of its own excluded from the per-page JS budget because it is route-scoped, and a link in the footer.

issues.problem: Thirteen of the twenty-plus routes have no layout spec at all — only a comma-separated block list. The worst gap is `/tools/snapflood/`, which §1 identifies as the flagship for the time-critical audience 4, and whose block list demands "the UFIS system diagram" — an asset that exists nowhere: not in the `Tools` tab, not in `Photos`, not in the Phase 5 shot list, not in "what we need from him", and with no named author, source data or licence. `/tools/` itself, called "the differentiator", is also unspecified.
issues.fix: Add §6.7 `/tools/` and §6.8 `/tools/snapflood/` at the same fidelity as §6.3. Add `body_doc_url` and `diagram` + `diagram_alt` to the `Tools` tab so a tool page has a prose source. Assign the UFIS diagram: either we draw it from his published system description (add 0.5 day to Phase 2 and put the source figure on the "from him" list), or the page ships with the SnapFlood screenshot and a numbered text description of the pipeline instead.

issues.problem: Trainee marking is specified three incompatible ways. §6.5: "People are rendered from the same collection as /publications/ supervision marks" (derived). §7.4: `author_marks` is a hand-typed `index:role` field. §9, in the professor-facing doc, says both — "put their position number in author_marks" under Add a publication, and "any paper they co-author is marked automatically" under Add a student. §9 also says the site adds a **★**, but §4.4 and §6.3 define the trainee marks as `* † ‡ #` and reserve ★ for the six selected papers.
issues.fix: Choose hand-typed `author_marks` (name-matching free-text author strings to People rows is unreliable and unspecified anyway), delete the "marked automatically" sentence from §9, correct "★" to "*" there, and add a validation column on `Publications` that resolves each `index:role` against the `People` roles enum with the same ✅/❌ formula used for `people_ids`.

issues.problem: Three collections are edited and never displayed. `Talks` has nine fields and appears on no route — the sitemap has no /talks/ and /about/'s blocks are bio, education, appointments, service, profile links, contact. `Awards` says "renders only if ≥1 row" but never says on which page. The `Manual` tab (Conference presentations / Invited seminars / Scientific activities / Products) has no display surface at all. He will type into three tabs and see nothing change, which is precisely the failure the §9 workflow is designed to avoid.
issues.fix: Add Talks and Awards as named blocks in the /about/ row of the sitemap ("→ selected talks (last 5, all on /about/cv/) → awards"), or add a `/talks/` route. Cut the `Manual` tab entirely (see the cut item) — its four categories duplicate Talks, Tools and Publications.

issues.problem: §5 states "About/Contact/CV/Join live in the footer and in in-page links". The specified footer in §6.2 contains: address, email, phone, Google Scholar, ORCID, CV (PDF), RSS, Colophon. There is no About link, no Join link and no Press link anywhere in the rendered layouts. `/about/` — which holds the long bio, education, appointments and service — is reachable from nothing, and `/press/` is reachable only by guessing the URL, which defeats a page whose entire purpose is a journalist finding it in five seconds during a flood.
issues.fix: Rewrite the footer spec as three labelled columns: **Contact** (address · email · phone) / **Elsewhere** (Scholar · ORCID · ResearchGate · LinkedIn · IITH) / **This site** (About · Join · Press kit · News · CV (PDF) · RSS · Colophon). Add a one-line "For journalists: press kit" under the masthead contact on /tools/snapflood/, since that is where audience 4 actually lands.

issues.problem: The brief contradicts its own counts in five places, and these are numbers that get hardcoded into visible copy. Alumni: "Eighteen alumni are listed" (§1), "fifteen graduated" (§6.2), "ALUMNI — 15 theses since 2019" (§6.5), "Eighteen graduates … the fifteen PhD/M.Tech alumni" (§12 Q4). Current students: "Nine current students" (§6.2) vs ten PhD names plus two M.Tech in §6.5 vs "12 people" in the §8.2 log. Publications: "a 56-item wall" (§1), "55 works" (§8.1), 39 pages. Selected papers: "max 8 TRUE" (§7.4) and "maximum eight" (§9) vs six everywhere it renders. Redirects: "all 13 published pages" over a 12-line table.
issues.fix: Do the count reconciliation as a Phase 1 deliverable and make every rendered count derived, never typed: the group teaser and alumni summary sentence compute from `People` rows, the publications link computes from non-excluded rows. Set `selected` max to 6 in both §7.4 and §9 and specify the build behaviour at 7+ (fail the row with a named error, do not silently truncate). Fix the 12-vs-13 redirect table by naming the missing Google Sites URL.

issues.problem: `Publications.theme` is a required enum that "matches a Research.slug". The five Research slugs are urban-flooding-hyderabad, streamflow-forecasting, monsoon-hydroclimatology, hydrologic-data-for-india, krishna-serayu-climate-extremes. The five filter chips on /publications/ are Urban flooding, Forecasting, Monsoon & climate, **Water management**, **Methods & tools** — two labels that map to no theme, and one theme (krishna-serayu) that maps to no chip. Separately /research/ renders "4 claim cards" and the home renders four claims while five theme pages exist, so /research/krishna-serayu-climate-extremes/ is rescued from orphanhood on the old site into a new orphan with no entry point in the IA.
issues.fix: Publish one canonical theme list. Either add `water-management` and rename `hydrologic-data-for-india` → `methods-and-tools` so chips and slugs are the same set (then /research/ shows six cards, not four), or decouple: add a separate `chip` field to `Publications` for the filter taxonomy and keep `theme` for page association. Also make `theme` optional — a Routledge book chapter and the NOAA-era HEFS papers will be force-fitted otherwise. Demote krishna-serayu to a row in the /research/ past-projects table (see the cut item).

issues.problem: The dark-mode media query ships empty: `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { /* below */ } }` — the dark values are only ever written under `[data-theme="dark"]`. A builder copying this block ships a site with no system dark mode at all. Separately, `data-theme` implies a user-facing toggle that appears in no layout (not in the masthead spec, not in the nav, not in the footer), has no persistence spec, no no-JS behaviour, and is not in the two-effect motion budget or the 20 KB JS budget.
issues.fix: Write the dark token values inside the media query and repeat them under `[data-theme="dark"]`, exactly as the brief's own theme-aware rule requires. Then decide the toggle: cut it and honour `prefers-color-scheme` only (recommended — it removes an unspecified control, a localStorage read, and an FOUC script from a site whose JS budget is 20 KB), or spec the control, its position, its accessible name, its persistence and its no-JS state.

issues.problem: The Tufte `<label>` + hidden-checkbox sidenote is adopted as a signature detail on research pages and blog posts. That pattern gives a control with no accessible name, no `aria-expanded`, and a reading order that jumps — it is the one signature element in the brief with a real accessibility cost, and §11's accessibility checks (keyboard pass, one page through the VoiceOver rotor) would catch it only by luck. Separately, blog images have **no alt-text source**: the Docs export produces no alt, the spec says the italic line under an image becomes the caption, and `Photos.alt` is required only for the Photos tab — so the build either ships blog images with empty alt or cannot ship them.
issues.fix: Use `<details><summary>` for sidenotes at every breakpoint, positioned into the right rail with CSS grid at ≥1100px and inline below it — same visual result, native semantics, keyboard and SR support for free, and one fewer responsive mode to test. For blog alt text: require a second italic line prefixed `Alt:` under each image in the Doc, validate its presence at build, and fail the post with a named error the same way a missing `Photos.alt` fails.

issues.problem: Empty states are specified only where they were easy. Unspecified: **blog with 0 posts** — /writing/ is one of six top-level nav items and Open Q11 contemplates "we ship the news feed only", but nothing says what happens to the nav item, /feed.xml, the sitemap or the home page in that case; **an alumnus with no `first_position`** — the row template prints "→ Now: [placement]" and the section header prints "Alumni are at [orgs]", both of which are meaningless when only 3 of 15 have replied; **`recruiting_deadline` blank** while the home block prints "Apply by 15 November"; **a person with no `sector`** while the alumni row prints a [Govt/Ind/Acad] tag; **0 search results**; **`/404` content**, which is listed in the sitemap and in Phase 4 with no spec whatsoever.
issues.fix: Add an "Empty and partial states" subsection to §6 with a row per case: blog with 0 published posts → the Writing nav item and /feed.xml are not emitted and the sitemap omits the route (build flag `BLOG_ENABLED`, derived from post count); alumnus with no placement → the row ends at the thesis title with no "Now:" fragment and no sector tag; the summary sentence renders only when ≥5 placements exist and names the count ("Eleven of fifteen are at …"); blank `recruiting_deadline` → the status sentence renders alone with no "Apply by"; 0 results → "No publications match. Show all 39."; and spec the /404 page (masthead, one sentence, links to Research, Publications, Group, Join, plus site search if kept).

issues.problem: Two URL-breaking edge cases have no policy. (1) `Slug` is listed without a ✓ in the Doc settings table, so it is optional and presumably derived from `Title` — meaning that renaming a Doc changes a published URL. (2) "To take a post down later, drag it into `Retired/`" — the post has already been in /feed.xml and the sitemap and has a live URL that feed readers and inbound links hold; nothing says whether it 404s, 410s, redirects, or stays up with a notice.
issues.fix: Make `Slug` required and frozen (the README says: never change this after publishing), and have the build fail on a slug change with a named error offering the old→new redirect line. Specify Retired behaviour: the page is removed from the index, feed and sitemap, and the URL serves a 410 with a "this post was withdrawn" note plus a link to /writing/ — or, if he prefers, stays live with a dated "withdrawn" banner. Pick one and put it in the failure-mode table.

issues.problem: Error row numbers are computed as `index + 2`, which is correct only when the header is row 1 and data starts at row 2. The §7 preamble says every tab has "a filled-in example in row 2 skipped by the build via a leading `#`", so real data starts at row 3. Depending on whether the skip happens before or after indexing, every error message is off by one — and the row number is the entire value of the error-reporting UX the brief is proudest of. §9's promise that a mistake gets him "an email in plain English telling you exactly which row to fix" fails silently.
issues.fix: State the rule explicitly: filter after indexing, carry the original sheet row on every parsed record as `_row = index + 2`, and add a test asserting that a bad value in sheet row 12 reports "row 12" with the example row present. Also specify that the leading `#` sentinel is checked in the first column only, so a `#` postdoc mark in `author_marks` cannot skip a row.

issues.problem: SEO is a stated requirement and Scholar indexing is specified in exhaustive detail, but ordinary page-level SEO is absent: there is no `<title>` template and no meta-description source for any route (39 paper pages, 5 theme pages, plus the rest), no canonical-URL policy, and no trailing-slash decision — every route in the sitemap carries a trailing slash while Cloudflare static assets will serve both forms, producing duplicate URLs for the same content. Separately, the Highwire meta block is specified only for the journal case, while the `type` enum has `chapter / conference / preprint / report / seminar`, which Scholar handles with different tags.
issues.fix: Add §8.6: title template per route type (`{page} — Satish Regonda` / `{paper title} — Satish Regonda`), description source per collection (`summary` for themes, `takeaway` or first 155 chars of `abstract` for papers, `dek` for posts), `<link rel=canonical>` self-referential on every page, and a trailing-slash rule enforced with a 301 in one direction. Add the meta mapping for non-journal types: `citation_inbook_title` + `citation_isbn` for chapters, `citation_conference_title` for conference papers, `citation_technical_report_institution` for reports, and omit Highwire entirely for `seminar`.

issues.problem: `--rail: 7rem` (112px) is the site's one repeated asymmetry, and §6.5 puts a sticky in-page navigation in that same left rail on /group/ with items including "Projects & funding" and "SnapFlood & tools". At the specified UI size (Public Sans 16.5px) those labels are ~140–160px and will wrap to two or three lines each, breaking the one geometry the brief says is repeated everywhere.
issues.fix: Either widen the /group/ rail to a named `--rail-nav: 11rem` and state that it is a deliberate second rail width used on exactly one page, or shorten the labels to fit 7rem ("What", "Themes", "Tools", "People", "Alumni", "Funding", "Join") and show them at the micro-label size. Say which in §4.3 so the grep rubric does not flag it.

issues.problem: Two specified layouts render fields the model does not have. §6.4's paper page ends with "[figure on a light plate, with caption in the right rail]" — `Publications` has no `figure`, `figure_alt` or `figure_caption` field, and reproducing a published journal figure is a rights problem the brief never raises. `/teaching/<code>/`'s blocks are "Syllabus PDF → topic outline → reading list → public notebooks" — the `Teaching` tab has `syllabus_url` and `tools` and none of the other three.
issues.fix: Cut the per-paper figure (see the cut item) or add the three fields plus a rights column. Add to `Teaching`: `outline` (long text or `body_doc_url`), `readings` (long text), `notebooks_url` — and note in §9 that a course page is only worth building for a course whose `page` box is ticked and whose outline is filled.

issues.problem: There are two divergent canonical banned-word lists, and the brief says the check runs in CI. §2 includes *groundbreaking* and *holistic (in the marketing sense)*; §11's list drops both and adds *let's connect*. A CI check needs exactly one list, and "holistic (in the marketing sense)" is not greppable.
